To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

capsaicin, an activator of sensory nerves, and calcitonin gene related peptide, an endogenous vasodilator, terminate long-lasting contractile effects of endothelin-1 in isolated resistance arteries by promoting dissociation of preformed endothelin-1/ETA receptor complexes.

capsaicin-induced release of endogenous calcitonin-gene related peptide (CGRP) from peri-vascular sensory-motor nerves dissociates pre-existing complexes of ET-1 with ETA-receptors and terminates the long-lasting effects of the peptide on mesenteric resistance artery contractility.
the contractile effects of endothelin-1 are terminated by calcitonin gene related peptide released from perivascular sensory-motor nerves.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how the cardiovascular system can terminate long-lasting effects of the paracrine peptide endothelin-1 (1).
the mechanisms of endothelin-1-induced contraction of resistance arteries.
the question of how the body is able to terminate the action of a long-lasting and highly potent vasoactive peptide.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the antagonism of ET-1 effects in cardiovascular system by CGRP and its receptor is a natural and physiological mechanism.
ET1/ETA complexes can be terminated by endogenous CGRP, which can be released upon activation of sensory nerves.
the ET-1/CGRP system is a key regulator of the ET-1-induced vascular tone and the balance between these two peptides is a major determinant of vascular function.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the quasi-irrevocable binding of ET-1 to ETA-receptor complexes can be selectively reversed by CGRP and that this mechanism can be exploited therapeutically.
the quasi-irresistible binding of endothelin-1 to ETA receptors can be selectively reversed by calcitonin gene related peptide.
the ET-1/ETAR complex can be dissociated by endogenous CGRP, which is released by stimuli of sensory-mor nerves.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the quasi-irrevrsibility of ET-1 binding to ETA-receptors is not an obstacle to antagonizing the peptide, because the binding can be terminated by endogeniously released CGRP.
the long-lasting contractile effects of endothelin-1 (i.e., ET-1) are mediated via the ETA-receptor and can be terminated by calcitonin gene related peptide (i.e., CGRP).
ET-receptor antagonism may be limited in its effectiveness by the quasi-irrevsibility of the ET-1/ET-receptor interaction.
